prompt: Some countries are considering reducing the standard working week from five days to four, with no reduction in pay. Do the advantages of this change outweigh the disadvantages?
essay:
The four-day week is usually argued as though it were one policy. It is at least two. In work whose output depends on thinking, a shorter week may cost nothing at all; in work whose output depends on presence, it costs exactly one day in five. Averaging those two cases produces a number that describes neither.

Where the first applies, the case is close to overwhelming. Much of a fifth day is absorbed by the fact that it exists: meetings expand, deadlines relax, and concentration in any case does not survive four days at full stretch. Employers who have tried it in this kind of work generally report that the same amount gets done, which is less a discovery about generosity than about how little the final day was producing. The employee gains a day and the employer loses nothing, which is a rare arrangement and worth taking seriously wherever it appears.

Where output tracks hours, none of that holds. A ward covered four days a week is a ward uncovered on the fifth, and the only remedy is more staff on the same pay, which is a straightforward cost increase and a large one. Nor is the compressed alternative a solution: four twelve-hour days is a different policy wearing the same name, and the fatigue it produces cancels most of what the change was for. Small employers with no spare capacity sit in the same position as hospitals, for the same reason.

So the advantages outweigh the disadvantages across a substantial part of the economy and clearly do not across the rest, and any honest answer has to say which is which. A default of four days, with the burden on employers to demonstrate that their work genuinely requires the fifth, would capture the gains where they exist without pretending that a hospital is an office. The mistake would be to legislate a single week for both and then be surprised by the results.
title: A four-day standard working week
